brief.title: 20-second spoken episode: the Inspector investigates a group-chat 'seen' with no reply
brief.objective: Viewer recognises themselves or a specific friend and follows for the next investigation.
constraints: One speaking character on screen; any second voice is off-camera.
Speech must fit timing at about 2.5 words per second.
negative_constraints: No real app logos or readable UI text.
Do not invent statistics about messaging behaviour.

evidence.claim: Speech totals about 34 words in 20 s, under 2.8 words/s in every scene.
The reversal in which the camera finds the Inspector's own fault fits the bible rule.
evidence.source: bible rule and selected premise P1

evidence.claim: Viewers will recognise themselves in the 'seen' situation.

premises.logline: At the living room side table, the Inspector cordons off a friend's 'seen' with safety-orange tape and builds a negligence case, then a gentle off-camera question reveals her own phone holds a stack of seen-and-unanswered messages from that same friend.
premises.audience_emotion: Guilty recognition with affection: everyone has been the one who saw it and meant to reply later.
premises.character_desire: A formal finding of fault against the friend who has not replied, so the world is orderly again.
premises.obstacle: The evidence is a single tick of silence; she needs it to amount to wrongdoing, and a second voice keeps asking neutral questions.
premises.escalation: Findings climb from 'delay' to 'negligence' to 'dereliction', each stated in a calmer voice. She tapes off the phone, then the thread, then the whole table, while the off-camera voice asks one mild question.
premises.surprise: The off-camera voice is the friend herself, asking only, 'Did you get my message about Saturday?' The Inspector's verdict is 'Inconclusive', and the camera slides to her own second phone, glowing under strips of her own tape.
premises.payoff: Rule delivered: she is exposed as the next offender. The two-finger clipboard tap lands on 'Inconclusive' as the camera finds her stack of identical, ignored threads.
premises.structure: Procedural accusation in a single locked frame, with a two-voice cross-examination, building to a reversal reveal on the camera move. Roughly 45 words of speech in 20 seconds.
premises.why_send_it: Send to the friend you keep leaving on 'seen' (or who keeps leaving you) with 'this is us'. It lets the sender accuse and confess in one forward.
premises.commercial_fit: None required; the brief has no commercial. Fully brand-safe: no real app, no readable UI, no endorsement.

premises.logline: In the hallway by the coat hooks, the Inspector narrates the forensic timeline of her own reply as she drafts, deletes and redrafts it aloud, never sending it, while the off-camera flatmate's patient 'Any news?' arrives for the third time.
premises.audience_emotion: Cringe-laugh at the overthinking reply spiral; self-recognition in the anxious drafter rather than the ignorer.
premises.character_desire: To produce one reply of perfect proportion: warm but not overeager, brief but not curt.
premises.obstacle: Each candidate reply has a measurable flaw: too many exclamation marks, too few, an emoji with ambiguous intent.
premises.escalation: Drafts get shorter and more bureaucratic ('Acknowledged.') while the delay grows from hours to days, marked by moving the hooks' coats one by one to a new hook as 'time passing'.
premises.surprise: The finished, perfect reply is simply 'ok', and she reads it aloud and approves it, but then sets the phone face-down in a coat pocket on the hook, 'for review'.
premises.payoff: She is the culprit of her own investigation: the final shot is the pocketed phone buzzing against the hook as the lamp dims.
premises.structure: Monologue-driven escalating montage in one hallway, rapid cut rhythm of draft, delete and verdict, with a hard-cut button.
premises.why_send_it: Send to the friend who writes and rewrites replies, with 'you at 2am'. Self-directed rather than accusatory.
premises.rejected_because: Mostly a single-note spiral with a weaker reversal; the culprit reveal is implied rather than caught by the camera.

premises.logline: The Inspector opens with the verdict already delivered ('The culprit saw it, and did not reply'), then rewinds through three exhibits that each point to a different suspect, until the final exhibit is a mirror-framed shot of herself.
premises.audience_emotion: Smug satisfaction turning to sheepish recognition: the accuser's lamp swings round.
premises.character_desire: To close the case in under twenty seconds with a clean conviction.
premises.obstacle: Her own chain of evidence keeps looping back through places she has been.
premises.escalation: Exhibit A (the quiet group thread), Exhibit B (a three-dot indicator that vanished), Exhibit C (a 'thumbs up' she insists is not a reply) each narrow the suspect pool until only one remains.
premises.surprise: Exhibit C is her own thumbs-up, deployed as a pretend reply last week; her lamp reflects in the glossy phone screen.
premises.payoff: Verdict stands, read in the same measured voice, but the culprit is her; the reflected lamp in the dark screen shows her face. Tap lands before she notices.
premises.structure: Reverse-chronological: verdict first, then evidence, then reflexive reveal. Hard pacing with three short exhibit beats.
premises.why_send_it: Send to the group chat itself, with 'Exhibit C: the thumbs up'. It names a shared, specific cheat.
premises.rejected_because: Strong concept but needs a mirror/reflection set-up and three exhibits inside 20 seconds, crowding the speech budget.

premises.logline: In the shared kitchen, a flatmate off-camera lists the Inspector's unanswered messages while she, stirring tea with total composure, issues formal 'rulings' that reclassify each one as 'not a message'.
premises.audience_emotion: Defensive-comic fondness: the pleasure of watching someone lawyer their way out of a small neglect.
premises.character_desire: To be found not guilty without ever admitting a single message existed.
premises.obstacle: The flatmate's evidence is dated and specific, and the voice never rises.
premises.escalation: Rulings go from 'a draft, not a message' to 'a meme, not a message' to 'a voice note is a weather event, not a message', each ruling sharper than the last.
premises.surprise: The flatmate stops listing and calmly says, 'I was only asking if you wanted tea.' The Inspector has been holding two mugs for the whole scene.
premises.payoff: She is the next offender: the mug she poured for the flatmate three messages ago is cold on the counter, caught in a slow push-in.
premises.structure: Two-hander dialogue (one on camera) in the kitchen with a deflating anticlimax; call-and-response rhythm.
premises.why_send_it: Send to the sibling or flatmate who never answers anything, with 'rulings'. Banter-forward, replies expected.
premises.rejected_because: The dialogue is the funniest on paper but the reveal (tea) drifts from the 'seen' topic the brief names.

premises.logline: The Inspector holds a vigil over a friend's silent thread at the side table, lamp trained on the phone, and quietly narrates the long wait as an unsolved disappearance until her own phone gives a small ping, and she flips it face-down.
premises.audience_emotion: Soft wistful humour: waiting is relatable and the ending is unresolved enough to prompt a reply from the viewer.
premises.character_desire: A reply, any reply, so the file can be closed.
premises.obstacle: The phone does nothing; she cannot act without breaking procedure.
premises.escalation: Lamp gets brighter, narration slower, a pencil is placed beside the phone as a 'marker'; time passes through a changing shadow.
premises.surprise: Her own phone pings with a message from someone she left unanswered, and her professional calm cracks into a single warm, disappointed sigh.
premises.payoff: Open ending: she turns the pinging phone face-down 'pending review', and the camera lingers on the dark, quiet table.
premises.structure: Slow-burn vigil, long takes, minimal speech (about 25 words), ending on an open loop rather than a verdict.
premises.why_send_it: Send to someone you are waiting on, as a wordless nudge. Low-key and kind.
premises.rejected_because: Too quiet for a TikTok hook, and the culprit rule is only a glance rather than a clear exposure.

hook_variants.first_frame: Locked eye-level shot at the living room side table: a phone lies face-up, its screen blank except a small generic 'seen' tick glyph (no logo, no readable text), already ringed with a square of safety-orange tape. The Inspector sits behind it, lamp on the phone, clipboard raised.
hook_variants.first_line_or_action: She presses the last strip of tape down with one finger, then says: 'Seen. Four hours ago. Case opened.'
hook_variants.rationale: A cordoned phone is legible muted in one second and the spoken 'seen, four hours' names the exact friend-offence, though it does not yet tease the self-reversal.

hook_variants.first_frame: Tight on the Inspector's face, brows level, lamp glowing, glasses low; foreground blur of an orange-taped phone. Burned-in subtitle: 'She saw it.'
hook_variants.first_line_or_action: Flat, measured: 'She saw my message. She did not reply. This is negligence.'
hook_variants.rationale: The accusation is instantly relatable and quotable, but a face-led frame is less distinctive than a taped object and the specificity rests on the line alone.

hook_variants.first_frame: Same locked side-table frame, but a second phone sits half out of shot at the edge of the table, face-down under a few torn strips of orange tape, while the Inspector faces the camera and the taped main phone.
hook_variants.first_line_or_action: Two-finger-free, deadpan: 'Everyone who leaves a friend on seen is a suspect.' Her eyes do not move toward the second phone.
hook_variants.rationale: The half-hidden taped second phone plants the rule payoff for the camera to find later and rewards a rewatch, at the cost of slightly diluting the one-second read of the main problem.

hook_variants.first_frame: Shared kitchen, eye-level: the Inspector stirs a mug with total composure, a second full mug steaming beside it, lamp on her chest. An off-camera voice is signalled only by her slow glance left.
hook_variants.first_line_or_action: Off-camera voice: 'You left me on seen.' The Inspector, still stirring: 'That is not a message. That is a draft.'
hook_variants.rationale: The instant deflection is funny and reads quickly with subtitles, but the stirring-tea frame is not obviously about a messaging problem without sound.

hook_variants.first_frame: Kitchen counter: a neat row of five mugs with small safety-orange tape labels in a straight line, the Inspector behind them holding a clipboard, a lamp spot on the row. No phone visible.
hook_variants.first_line_or_action: She taps nothing, speaks in her measured cadence: 'Five messages. Zero messages. Allow me to explain.'
hook_variants.rationale: The row of labelled mugs is visually striking and promises an escalating ruling ritual, but with no phone the 'seen with no reply' problem is vague for the first second.

hook_variants.first_frame: Kitchen, the Inspector facing camera and holding two mugs, one in each hand, as if about to deliver one; her lamp is lit and her expression neutral. A pencil-thin strip of orange tape marks a line on the counter in front of her.
hook_variants.first_line_or_action: Off-camera: 'You never replied to anything.' Inspector, evenly: 'Define replied.'
hook_variants.rationale: 'Define replied' is a sharply shareable lawyering line to send to a flatmate, and the two mugs seed the reveal, but the topic anchor is verbal rather than visual.

selected.rationale: H3 keeps P1's exact 'seen with no reply' topic, shows a taped-off problem the viewer reads in one second, and quietly plants the second taped phone so the bible's rule (the camera notices before she does) pays off on the reveal and invites a rewatch. The trade-off against the runner-up H1 is a slightly less clean first-second read of the main phone in return for the planted payoff and a more shareable line aimed at 'everyone who leaves a friend on seen'; H1 is the safer fallback if testing shows the second phone clutters the frame.

script.title: Seen
script.synopsis: At the side table the Inspector tapes off a friend's 'seen' and escalates it from delay to dereliction; the friend's gentle off-camera question stops her, her verdict is 'Inconclusive', and the camera slides to her own second phone under her own tape, with a stack of ignored threads. The friend notes it is her sixth.

beats.beat: Locked frame: taped phone, half-hidden taped second phone, accusation to everyone who leaves a friend on seen
Four hours becomes delay becomes negligence
Dereliction, taping the whole table edge
Off-camera friend asks about Saturday; verdict 'Inconclusive' with the clipboard tap
Camera finds her own taped second phone with a stack of ignored threads
Friend: 'That's my sixth one, you know.' Inspector exhales

evidence.originality: Cordoning off a 'seen' with crime-scene tape and escalating delay to negligence to dereliction in an ever-calmer voice, then reversing onto her own taped phone, is a fresh, specific take rather than a generic texting joke.
evidence.hook: The first line names the viewer's exact guilt ('Everyone who leaves a friend on seen is a suspect') over an instantly legible taped-phone image, though the planted second phone is half out of frame and the opening line is a flat statement, not a question or a surprise.
evidence.coherence: The escalation, the friend's Saturday question and the 'Inconclusive' verdict lead cleanly to the reveal, but the second phone goes from face-down in S4 to face-up and glowing in S5, and the friend's closing 'my sixth one' is ambiguous about whose messages are unanswered.
evidence.identity: The glasses, aubergine jacket, chest lamp, lanyard clipboard, deadpan flat delivery and the single two-finger tap are held consistently across all five scenes, and the warm-disappointment break fits the bible's tone.
evidence.audiovisual: Each scene specifies lighting, foley (tape peel, clipboard knock), room tone, voice placement and captions, and the camera slide to the second phone makes the payoff a visual beat, though there is no music or sonic sting at the button.
evidence.feasibility: A single continuous 20 s unit with an in-shot hand-pushed slider move, a prop that flips state mid-take, a near-silent mid-air tape hold and a precise 40 cm slide are risky for current video generation and will likely need takes or a fallback.
evidence.grounding: There are no invented statistics, no real app logos or readable UI (blank grey bubbles and a generic tick glyph), two locations at most (one used), and one on-camera speaker with the second voice off-camera, all within the brief's constraints.
evidence.commercial_fit: The brief has no commercial and the packet correctly adds none, and the share-driven CTA ('send this to the friend you left on seen') and follow prompt match the stated objective and platform.

creative.summary: A distinctive, shareable premise with a strong accusation-to-confession reversal, consistent character identity and thorough audiovisual direction. It is weakened by a prop-state inconsistency between S4 and S5, a slightly ambiguous button line, and a continuous-take slider move that carries generation risk.
creative.top_fix: Make the second phone's state consistent (face-down or face-up in both S4 and S5) and sharpen the final line so it clearly means 'you have left me unanswered six times', or else split the S4 slide into a separate generation unit to reduce take risk.

repetition.note: Lexical similarity only; a reviewer must judge whether flagged overlap is identity (allowed) or a repeated joke/plot/device (not). 'devices' covers hook mechanism, props, lighting language, off-camera-voice use and the surprise device.
